items.title: Plane may have broken apart ahead of deadly Florida jet crash, say investigators
items.summary: The National Transportation Safety Board also believes weather could have been a factor in the crash, but warns it is too early to determine the cause.
items.content:
The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) says it will investigate whether parts of a jet that crashed in Florida broke off before it nose-dived and exploded, killing all nine people on board.

The Learjet 60, which was travelling from Austin, Texas to the Bahamas on Sunday, crashed on a street nine miles (14 km) from President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.

A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old copilot, were among those who died.

The NTSB said on Monday that it would also investigate to what extent ice and turbulence may have been contributing factors.

It confirmed that, after the jet took off from Austin, the crew transmitted to air traffic control that they were encountering ice and moderate turbulence.

"We are picking up precipitation, requesting to climb to 37,000 feet if able," the crew said.

NTSB member Tom Chapman said that less than 30 seconds later, the plane began to descend and the crew issued a mayday call.

The transmission then became "unintelligible", he said, adding that: "Sadly, all aboard were lost."

The NTSB said that ice and turbulence were factors in the crash but that determining its probable cause will be a "lengthy investigatory process".

Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.

As part of the investigation, the NTSB is working with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), representatives from Learjet as well as meteorologists and air traffic control experts.

Recovering the wreckage from the crater on the roadway will be a "daunting challenge", said Timothy Monville, an air safety investigator with the safety board.

Flight analysis indicates the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.

In air traffic control audio, a crew member can be heard declaring an emergency, shouting "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".

About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last remark from the cockpit appears to be "we're out of time".

The seven people killed who were travelling as passengers were identified in a joint statement from their families as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma and Charlie - as well as Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina.

The pilot was named in media reports as Jeffery Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the copilot.

As well as those killed, one man on the ground sustained a leg injury when the plane nosedived onto the street.

The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the crash happened on Military Trail, a six-lane road lined with businesses and restaurants.

Images from the crash scene show a large fiery crater in the middle of a residential suburban street.

The debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area, officials told a news conference on Monday, possible evidence that the plane broke up before it hit the ground.

Unverified footage posted on social media shows what appears to be a dash-camera recording of the moment of the crash.

Trump was at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday morning, and departed from an airport nearby on Air Force One about an hour before the crash.

items.title: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
items.summary: Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in any offensive operations.
items.content:
Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal.

Nearly 3,000 military personnel from 12 European nations will take part in the rehearsal in neighbouring Poland this month.

Plans for a reassurance force for Ukraine were set out last year as one of the long-term security guarantees being proposed by European nations.

But there are still more questions than answers as to how such a military force might work in practice. Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in offensive operations or be involved in peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring missions.

Nor would they be operating under the command of Nato or on the front line.

Officials say their presence would be to provide reassurance to Ukraine and to help rebuild its armed forces.

The US has been involved in discussions, but is not contributing to the mission.

Russia has already voiced opposition to foreign troops being stationed in Ukraine and, last year, President Vladimir Putin said they would be "legitimate targets".

Western officials have declined to spell out the rules of engagement if any international troops were to be attacked in Ukraine. Though they say the force would be able to defend itself.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the exercise showed Britain, France and their allies were stepping up preparation for the day when peace came to Ukraine.

He said: "This is not a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops."

Lt Gen Tom Bateman, the UK commander of the Multi National Force – Ukraine (MNF-U), said the exercise represented an important step in translating political commitments into credible military readiness.

He said it was a "real, capable, readily deployable force that represented a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine's long-term stability and security".

Exercise Koalicja - which takes place from 9-22 November - will be a rehearsal of how to move, protect and supply a force in Ukraine. It will also be a test of their command and control to ensure troops from different countries can work together.

Some 2,800 military personnel will take part across land, sea and air, with the UK contribution including 300 troops and a pair of RAF Typhoons.

Fighter jets will simulate how they would reassure commercial aircraft once Ukraine's skies can be reopened.

Turkey has agreed to lead the maritime mission, with the eventual goal to clear mines and allow the resumption of trade in the Black Sea.

As well as the UK, troops will come from France, Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey.

However, Western officials could not comment on the final make-up and shape of the force that could be deployed to Ukraine if the fighting stops.

In the past, military experts have suggested that Western nations might have to send tens of thousands of troops to Ukraine to guarantee its security.

Officials acknowledge that the countries' commitment and contributions will depend on the circumstances of a cessation of hostilities and individual nations' political decisions.

It is also unclear what training role Western forces could provide to battle hardened Ukraine.

Ukrainian soldiers are already in high demand training Nato forces - passing on their expertise in drone warfare.

Above all, Russia has shown no sign of wanting to end its war.

items.title: Midterm Usa, la Corte suprema boccia la richiesta di Trump di bloccare 20mila voti in California
items.summary: L’amministrazione guidata dal tycoon aveva ipotizzato che le schede per corrispondenza fossero state consegnate a persone non in possesso della cittadinanza americana
items.content: Vigilia delle elezioni di midterm agitata. La Corte suprema Usa , senza la registrazione di alcun voto contrario, ha respinto in serata la richiesta dell' amministrazione Trump di imporre alla California di accantonare ventimila schede elettorali per corrispondenza sull'ipotesi che possano essere state consegnate a persone non cittadine americane. Il provvedimento, privo di firma e di motivazioni, è giunto lo stesso giorno in cui i legali dell'amministrazione si sono rivolti alla Corte dopo che una corte d'appello federale aveva rigettato la tesi dell'amministrazione secondo cui le autorità californiane avrebbero dovuto sequestrare le schede per sottoporle a ulteriori verifiche.

items.title: Indonesia's toxic haze is giving its neighbours a political headache
items.summary: Governments in Singapore and Malaysia are split between anxious citizens and an irascible neighbour.
items.content:
The haze billowing out from wildfires in the Indonesian regions of Kalimantan, Papua and Sumatra knows no borders.

Carried by winds to nearby Singapore and Malaysia, the toxic smog has in recent weeks impacted populations across maritime South East Asia, triggering respiratory illnesses and headaches.

It's also giving the region's governments a different kind of headache - split between the mounting frustrations of their citizens and the risk of souring diplomatic ties with Indonesia.

"People are fed up, angry and anxious," Eugene Tan, associate professor of law at the Singapore Management University, tells the BBC. "The governments have to respond to them, or else what is more an external issue has become an internal one with ample headroom for politicisation."

Indonesia's wildfires are a yearly occurrence, widely associated with industrial-scale land clearing to make way for crops like oil palm.

But the blazes this year have been particularly difficult to tame due to a strong El Niño, which has exacerbated drought conditions in the country's forests and peatlands.

Whereas previous haze episodes in Singapore and Malaysia have typically lasted for a few days, this time it stretched into weeks.

In Malaysia, locals started a boycott of Indonesian products in protest against the haze, after lawmaker Syed Saddiq called for sanctions on companies linked to the wildfires and said Malaysians should "treat them as an outcast in the region".

There have also been complaints in Singapore, a country that has come to expect seamless efficiency from its leaders.

"There appears to be the view that the government dropped the ball in dealing with the haze, given that it was known that the El Niño weather phenomenon would be severe and that early warning was given," says Tan.

"Clearly, Singaporeans expect the government to decisively deal with the polluters."

Singapore's government, for its part, has made it clear that the haze problem is a priority.

Hundreds of haze shelters have been set up across the island, and masks are being distributed to children, the elderly and other vulnerable residents.

Authorities have also said they're looking to strengthen existing haze legislation and are investigating 10 Singapore-registered companies for potential links to the wildfires in Indonesia.

Last week, Singapore's foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan met Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto in Jakarta for what the former described as "honest" and "sincere" conversations that produced "constructive approaches".

The meeting came as both countries announced they would set up a joint task force to deal with the haze - an apparent détente after weeks of simmering bilateral tensions.

As the haze spiralled into yet another crisis for Prabowo's beleaguered administration, some officials pushed back against criticism .

One senior official ruffled feathers when he said the wildfires were out of human control and that oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".

That remark was "disappointing" and "not right", according to Singaporean senior minister K Shanmugam - a rare rebuke from the city state, which prides itself on its diplomatic prowess.

"The haze is affecting our health seriously, and it's really unacceptable," Shanmugam told reporters. Since the haze impacts citizens on both sides of the border, there should not be "any bilateral issues" in addressing it, he added.

"The Indonesian public is suffering as well , and it is in Indonesia's interest as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."

Days later, Indonesia announced it would reduce gas exports to Singapore, citing domestic energy needs - a move that many saw as retaliation to Singapore's rhetoric.

To be sure, Indonesia has faced recent electricity shortages in parts of the country. Singapore also says the reduction, which amounts to less than 2% of its total daily demand, will have little impact on its gas supply.

But the abrupt announcement came just days after Indonesia's energy minister warned that they could halt gas exports to countries that don't "respect Indonesia". That same day, Prabowo made reference to "countries that like to insult Indonesia" when talking about the wildfires.

"It's a tired playbook of using Singapore as the bogeyman, driven by the 'abang-adik' [big brother-little brother] syndrome," Tan says, referring to a historical dynamic that Singapore's leaders have long tried to shrug off: the expectation that it should defer to its larger neighbours.

"Singapore leaders expressing concerns about the haze and how it affects the people of both countries have been taken to mean that Singapore has been disrespectful to its neighbour."

In contrast, Malaysia's official rhetoric on the haze has been relatively muted.

Its foreign minister Mohamad Hasan has ruled out lodging a formal diplomatic protest with Indonesia or taking legal action, saying such actions "would mean we were prepared to sever relations".

For now, Malaysia has agreed to explore a memorandum of understanding with Indonesia to strengthen wildfire prevention efforts.

It would also rely on diplomatic mechanisms, Mohamad said - like the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.

The agreement, which came into effect in 2003, commits members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to collaborate on tackling the recurring haze.

But many see it as toothless, as it is unable to punish agricultural companies linked to wildfires or to force individual governments to do so.

The agreement has turned out to be "just not worth the paper it was signed on", says James Chin, professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.

"The moment the haze disappears, the moment the political pressure's off, it's back to business as usual."

In 2016, Asean countries had set a goal to eliminate haze in the region by 2020. When that deadline drifted quietly by, they set a new target of achieving the goal by 2030 instead.

Complicating Malaysia's position is the fact that it is also a major palm oil producer. The commodity is often linked to commercial "slash-and-burn" practices that are widely blamed for the region's wildfires.

Malaysia has at times dealt with acute haze stemming from blazes on local land.

In 2019, when Malaysia pointed to hotspots in Indonesia's peatlands as the cause of the haze shrouding the region, Indonesian authorities pointed the finger back at Malaysia, claiming the smog came from their side.

"As long as we place a lot of importance on oil palm planting, [the haze] is going to recur," says Ei Sun Oh, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia.

And even if Malaysia were to speak up, Oh adds, it's unlikely to wield the same "leverage" over Indonesia as Singapore, which is Indonesia's largest foreign investor and an offshore financial hub for many wealthy Indonesians.

For now, Malaysia "doesn't want to unduly provoke Indonesia", says Oh.

"The government is just wringing their hands till the wind blows [the problem] over. Because eventually it will blow over."

items.title: L’attacco russo contro il centro umanitario ucraino di Komyshuvakha
items.summary: È stato fatto in due momenti, per colpire anche i soccorritori: almeno 29 persone sono state uccise
items.content:
Martedì 2 novembre la Russia ha bombardato una scuola adibita a centro per la distribuzione di aiuti umanitari a Komyshuvakha, nella parte meridionale della regione ucraina di Zaporizhzhia. Almeno 29 persone sono state uccise, altre cinque sono state ferite, e ci sono 48 dispersi.

Il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky ha detto che è stata usata una tecnica conosciuta con l’espressione inglese double tap , doppio fuoco, e funziona così: bombardano, lasciano passare qualche minuto in modo che arrivino i soccorritori e poi bombardano di nuovo la stessa area per uccidere sia l’obiettivo iniziale sia chi arriva dopo. La tecnica del double tap è stata perfezionata dai piloti dei bombardieri russi durante la guerra civile in Siria, dove ci furono decine di casi documentati, e poi è stata applicata durante l’invasione russa su larga scala in Ucraina per fiaccare il morale della popolazione.

Zelensky ha spiegato che gli aerei russi hanno lanciato su Komyshuvakha un primo attacco che ha colpito la scuola, intrappolando al suo interno civili e addetti alla distribuzione degli aiuti. Dopodiché, durante il secondo attacco, hanno colpito il rifugio in cui la popolazione si era riparata. Durante il secondo bombardamento sono state sganciate nove bombe, ciascuna contenente 1,36 tonnellate di esplosivo. Tra le persone morte ci sono due soccorritori e quattro agenti di polizia. Oltre alla scuola sono stati colpiti una palestra e un camion dei pompieri.

Secondo il presidente ucraino «i russi non potevano non sapere che ogni settimana gli abitanti rimasti a Komyshuvakha ricevevano aiuti umanitari proprio in quel luogo». Zelensky ha poi scritto che le modalità dell’azione sono una nuova prova del fatto che «la Russia non vuole né una de-escalation né una pace realmente giusta».

L’attacco è avvenuto un giorno dopo la scadenza della tregua umanitaria che Russia e Ucraina avevano negoziato per permettere l’evacuazione dei civili e l’ingresso di aiuti umanitari a Oleshky, una cittadina nella zona meridionale dell’Ucraina occupata dai russi dal 2022 e che da mesi non riceveva rifornimenti di cibo e medicine.

Zelensky ha detto che l’operazione umanitaria a Oleshky aveva aperto «una fase in cui i passi successivi avrebbero potuto dimostrare che erano possibili progressi verso la pace», mentre con questi nuovi attacchi, «la Russia sta lanciando un segnale del tutto opposto», ovvero di voler «provocare altre vittime». Da qui l’appello di Zelensky alla comunità internazionale: «Dev’esserci una risposta dal mondo, una risposta forte e decisa».

Zaporizhzhia è una delle quattro regioni ucraine che il presidente russo Vladimir Putin dice di aver annesso nel 2022, sebbene le sue forze non abbiano mai conquistato il capoluogo. La linea del fronte si estende in tutta la regione e i combattimenti continuano da anni.

items.title: L'Atalanta crolla in casa con il Parma, la curva contesta Sarri e calciatori
items.summary: Gli emiliani si impongono 3-0. Prima vittoria di Gilardino
items.content:
Il Parma di Gilardino conquista la prima vittoria della nuova gestione, a discapito dell'Atalanta di mister Sarri: il ciclo del nuovo tecnico stenta ancora a decollare. Quinta sconfitta per l'allenatore che 'predica' una difesa a quattro e a zona che continua a non funzionare. Termina 3-0 per i ducali tra i fischi della Curva Nord verso squadra e tecnico. Gelata da Fabbian a 6' dall'intervallo dopo un primo tempo dominato, la squadra bergamasca sfiora il pari con Zalewski per poi andare sotto 2-0 ad inizio ripresa a causa di una maldestra autorete di Zappacosta: infine prende il terzo gol da Lontani che si cava lo sfizio del tunnel a Pasalic. Di fronte ai ducali molto ordinati e pronti alle ripartenze, i nerazzurri accumulano una serie di occasioni che però non trasformano.

L'avvio è di marca locale, con De Ketelaere protagonista su scambio con Rowe al 6'. Daffara chiude in angolo, mentre due minuti più tardi Zappacosta gli contende palla in posizione irregolare sul filtrante di Zalewski poi ripreso da Ederson per l'appoggio in porta annullato a Krstovic. Intorno al quarto d'ora un'altra fuga del belga dei nerazzurri dalla metà campo si conclude con un sinistro stavolta largo. Gli emiliani sono ridotti a contenere: dal ventesimo fino intorno alla mezz'ora ci provano senza mira Ederson da fuori, Zappacosta calciando in fallo laterale il pallone lanciatogli basso da Scaslvini e Krstovic, contrastato da Troilo in angolo sul passaggio a centro area di Rowe. Gli ospiti, conquistato il primo corner al 35' sull'asse Valeri-Lontani, riescono a concludere di testa con Delprato che gira sull'esterno della rete la battuta di Sierro. Poi s'accende Fabbian, che prima costringe Zappacosta ad anticipare di testa in corner Lontani appostato sul secondo palo e quindi gira in porta con la stessa specialità la traiettoria di Sierro dall'angolo sinistro, infilandosi tra Krstovic e Scalvini. Si esauriscono i 2' di recupero con un sinistro al volo parato da Daffara a Zalewski. La ripresa si apre con un anticipo a Lontani da parte di Zappacosta che infila però la propria porta al termine di una azione che parte da Fabbian e arriva a El Bilal Touré con palla messa davanti al secondo palo. Al decimo Rowe riceve da De Ketelaere davanti al lato corto dell'area piccola, ma il suo destro aperto di piatto è deviato in angolo da Daffara. Al 13' Lontani firma il tris aprendo nell'angolino il destro dal limite: Bernasconi rinvia corto di testa il lancio di Ndiaye, subentrato a Drobnic, sui piedi di Fabbian che innesca l'attaccante diciottenne. Al 26' il nuovo entrato Ordóñez manca il quarto gol su scarico al limite di Touré. Poco prima una parata di Daffara su Krstovic, attivato dalla sponda di Pasalic su cross a rientrare di Zalewki. Poi traversa alta di Pasalic su iniziativa di Idele e una mezza occasione ancora del montenegrino che svetta centralmente su un cross del 2007 di fascia che ha esorido anche in A dopo la presenza in Conference League contro il Pafos. Finisce quindi tra i fischi della Curva Nord che contesta i calciatori, intonando i cori "meritiamo di più" e "l'Atalanta siamo solo noi". Tra tre giorni c'è il Kairat Almaty, con la panchina atalantina che appare un po' traballante.

items.title: The SEC Should Block Anthropic's IPO to Protect the Public
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.techpolicy.press/the-sec-should-block-anthropics-ipo-to-protect-the-public/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50344919 Points: 348 # Comments: 258
items.content:
Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts .

Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings , extensive use of financial engineering , and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies.

That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut.

The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is.

Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent financial disclosures revealed nearly $900 billion in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth slowed to a crawl over the summer.

Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due.

The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its amended registration statement reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models.

Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts in a legal and practical sense : they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so.

Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land on Anthropic’s balance sheet. With the company continuing to negotiate further massive infrastructure and compute contracts , Anthropic may well end the year with a trillion dollars or more in contractual commitments.

Generating the revenues necessary to meet those obligations would be, to say the least, quite difficult for any company. But the margins of AI model developers are being squeezed by several forces that will make that task extraordinarily challenging for Anthropic.

First, it isn’t clear that there is nearly enough demand for generative AI products and services to justify Anthropic’s spending. Multiple studies , including from organizations notable for their bullishness on AI, suggest LLMs are not accelerating productivity or otherwise generating positive returns on investment for most businesses . Worryingly for enterprise-focused Anthropic, one study found that the number of Americans using AI at work fell significantly between the summers of 2025 (46%) and 2026 (33%).

Anthropic’s spending commitments suggest that the company believes it will be able to convince businesses to pay for ever-larger and more expensive models. But there are growing signs that most businesses are not interested in paying for more powerful and expensive models. When Anthropic released its much-hyped Fable 5 frontier model this summer, its commercial reception was tepid .

Even if a future Anthropic model captivates businesses, the company would run into a second obstacle: the AI industry’s frenzied competition. Anthropic is part of a crowded Silicon Valley ecosystem where numerous well-heeled corporations (including Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and SpaceX, along with Anthropic) offer generative AI models that are largely indistinguishable in their quality and capabilities. As a result, AI companies can quickly offer competing products whenever a rival identifies a use case that shows even a hint of commercial potential.

In such an environment, companies can rarely afford to raise prices because doing so will prompt customers simply to switch to a rival. The rush to grab customers ahead of their IPOs led Anthropic and OpenAI to launch a price war this summer that remains ongoing. Competition from Chinese companies offering open-weights models puts further downward pressure on prices, as does the increasing availability of models that can run locally on phones and laptops — no expensive data centers required.

That leads to the third problem: the extraordinarily high costs of the chips and data centers needed to train and run AI models, which put powerful and continuous upward pressure on Anthropic’s costs. Between the chips, servers, networking equipment, electricity and cooling infrastructure, construction costs, and other expenses, a 1 gigawatt (GW) data center costs an estimated $31 billion , and the prices for some components are soaring.

That is for 1 GW. Anthropic has committed to 15 GW of data center capacity in the coming years and the company estimates it will ultimately need 20-25 GW, which explains the company’s half-trillion-plus dollars in spending commitments.

And that is just the cost of the physical infrastructure. Once a data center is up and running, training AI models entails using tens of thousands of chips running in parallel that require massive amounts of energy to power, run hot, and need to be kept cool. Moreover, each time someone prompts a model to answer a question, create an image, or perform a task, additional computational power, energy, and cooling are needed to process the query and generate a response or complete the task.

Finally, there are external factors that are delaying data center construction and piling on additional costs. The fierce and still-rising backlash to AI in general and data centers in particular across the country has scuttled a number of data center projects and delayed many others. Every delay limits the computational capacity Anthropic is counting on to generate the revenue it will desperately need, and rising costs due to the Iran War and supply-chain challenges could drive Anthropic’s operational costs still higher.

Anthropic will further pad its cash reserves if its IPO is successful, but the brutal economics of its business are not likely to improve anytime soon. Even if demand picks up significantly, intense competition will apply unrelenting downward pressure on prices even as high costs and resource constraints squeeze it from the opposite direction. That is a deadly mix for Anthropic in light of its slowing revenue growth and massive off-balance-sheet debts, a vast and immovable fixed cost.

If Anthropic were to go public now, it would pile additional risk onto a stock market that is already historically overvalued and disproportionately concentrated in a handful of tightly interconnected mega-cap companies from the tech sector. That has already created a risk of a historically damaging stock market crash ; never before has such a huge amount of wealth depended on the performance of a small number of companies whose fortunes are inextricably linked. Adding another huge, unprofitable tech giant to public exchanges would exacerbate both of those factors and create a higher risk of contagion if (or, rather, when) Anthropic reaches a financial precipice.

It also would mean that an ever-larger share of the fallout from a potentially devastating AI crash would fall on ordinary people. As a private company, Anthropic’s shares are overwhelmingly owned by corporate insiders, tech giants, and venture capitalists. Once the company goes public and shares start getting funneled into 401(k)s, retirement accounts, and index funds, it will be workers, retirees, and retail investors that are increasingly left holding the bag when the forces squeezing Anthropic’s margins start to bite.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has the power to stop that from happening. The agency can delay or stop companies from going public if it believes a company’s registration statement is “ on its face incomplete or inaccurate in any material respect .” That legislative language might as well have been written with Anthropic in mind, considering that the company’s prospectus includes only unaudited financial results for the period where it claims the greatest revenue growth, relegates its most significant future obligations to the footnotes of its registration statement, and has continued to announce new 11-digit financial commitments as its IPO approaches.

items.title: SLAC researchers find proof of altermagnetism, a new magnetic phase
items.summary: Article URL: https://www6.slac.stanford.edu/news/2026-10-29-slac-researchers-find-proof-altermagnetism-new-magnetic-phase Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50344224 Points: 74 # Comments: 9
items.content:
For decades, physicists recognized only two types of magnetism that occur in materials without external influence: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. Today, in findings published in Science , a team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory has delivered conclusive experimental proof of a third magnetic phase called altermagnetism.

“In the past few years, scientists have observed phenomena that don't fit neatly into the ferromagnetism-antiferromagnetism dichotomy,” explained lead author Daniel Jost , associate scientist at SLAC and Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences . “Researchers have been compiling evidence of a third type of magnetism that bridges the qualities of these two classes. We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase – altermagnetism – is real.”

Building on previous studies, this research confirmed that manganese telluride (MnTe) is an altermagnet – a new class of magnet that exhibits properties of both ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. Their results showed direct experimental evidence of chirality – an asymmetric magnetic structure, akin to a spiral staircase or a screw – in the spins of an altermagnetic candidate material.

Identifying these unique materials could allow researchers to manipulate their properties in ways that make them ideal candidates for advanced electronics, with applications including quantum technologies, memory devices and data centers.

To most of us, magnetism is a tangible force: It’s what holds a child's artwork to a refrigerator door and points a compass needle north. But to a physicist, magnetism is more complex. It’s a quantum property of a material, and not all magnetic materials have a directly observable magnetic effect.

In physics, a material is considered magnetic if its electrons’ spins – their internal angular momentum, which can be either “up” or “down” – are polarized, or ordered in a specific pattern.

In ferromagnets, all electronic spins point the same direction (up-up-up or down-down-down), creating an observable magnetic field. Humans have known about and made use of this class of magnets since ancient times. In 1933, scientists discovered another type of material with polarized spins. Antiferromagnets have alternating electronic spins (up-down-up-down) that cancel each other out, producing no net magnetic effect.

For nearly 90 years, this two-category system dominated our understanding of magnetism.

But in recent years, researchers have noticed that some materials don’t fit neatly into either category. Certain materials seemed to exhibit features of both antiferromagnetism, such as alternating spin configuration with no net magnetization, and ferromagnetism, such as the ability to use spin currents . These behaviors were once thought to be mutually exclusive.

In 2022, researchers proposed the term “altermagnets” to label this wily class of materials.

We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase – altermagnetism – is real.

To explain this behavior, researchers postulated that altermagnets exhibit an alternating spin polarization (up-down-up-down), much like conventional antiferromagnets, but with a crucial twist: the crystal lattice structure surrounding the “up” spins is rotated relative to the lattice surrounding the “down” spins. This geometric twist is a break in symmetry that could give rise to their unusual behavior.

“By 2024, there were some factors that spoke strongly in favor of altermagnetism being real,” Jost said, “but there was still a missing piece to the puzzle.”

That missing piece was experimental evidence of chirality in an altermagnetic candidate material. Chirality, often referred to as “handedness,” means a material cannot be superimposed on a mirror image of itself, just like a left hand cannot fit into a right-handed glove.

Chirality offers a clever way to distinguish subtle, quantum-level differences between antiferromagnets and suspected altermagnets: While an altermagnetic material would have alternating spins (up-down-up-down) like an antiferromagnet, the geometric twists in its lattice would give the material’s electronic and magnetic structure a distinct handedness that conventional antiferromagnets lack.

Jost’s team chose to investigate chirality in MnTe – a material considered antiferromagnetic for decades until a few years ago when it was suspected to be altermagnetic. The team brought it to the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in France, to a beamline known for its ability to generate highly controlled polarized X-ray beams.

“Chiral materials scatter left-handed polarized X-ray beams differently than they do right-handed beams,” explained Jost. “Non-chiral materials would scatter each beam of light the same way.”

By scattering circularly polarized X-rays from the material and comparing how it responded to left- versus right-handed light, they teased out a clear chiral signal that shouldn’t exist in a conventional antiferromagnet.

“This chiral signature gave us the solid experimental ground to say altermagnetism stands in a class of its own,” Jost said. The initial experiment was completed in 2024; the team repeated their experiment in early 2025, confirming their earlier results.

“This technique helped us confirm that manganese telluride was really exhibiting altermagnetic properties,” said Rachel Nickel, postdoctoral scientist with ESRF, a co-author who helped design and conduct the experiment on the ID32 beamline. “Altermagnetism was only proposed a few years ago, and the rapid progress in confirming these models is incredible.”

This discovery has big implications for the field of spintronics, where researchers are leveraging the polarized spin of magnetic materials to design next-generation electronics.

Where traditional computing technologies use only an electron’s charge to store and move information, spintronics takes advantage of both an electron’s charge and its spin, giving researchers an additional control knob. Spintronic devices have the potential to be faster, be more robust and significantly decrease power consumption in computing and data centers.

Researchers have had some success with spintronic devices, but that success has been limited by the nature of ferro- and antiferromagnetism.

“Ferromagnets are too easily influenced by magnetic fields,” Jost explained. “If you have a permanent magnet in your pocket and walk by a spintronic device built with ferromagnets, you could start flipping the bits, scrambling the information stored there. Antiferromagnets fix that problem, but they are practically invisible – so you can’t easily read the data stored in them or use them to drive efficient spin currents.”

“Altermagnets combine the best of both,” Jost said. “They have zero net magnetization, so they're stable, but they still have the capability to generate spin-polarized currents needed to easily extract information. That gives you an additional degree of freedom to work with.”

Future research will explore how altermagnetic states can be influenced and controlled using light and electricity to enhance their usefulness in spintronic solutions for quantum technologies, memory devices and data centers.

This research is supported in part by the DOE Office of Science.

items.title: Musk pumps $446m into US midterms, as campaign spending set to 'shatter' records
items.summary: The 2026 campaign is projected to cost nearly $12bn - BBC Verify looks into where all that money has come from.
items.content:
The US midterms campaign is set to be the most expensive on record - with the total cost projected to reach nearly $12bn (£9bn), according to Open Secrets, an independent organisation that tracks campaign finance.

Most of the spending is driven by outside political groups - known as Super Political Action Committees (Super Pacs) - pouring large sums of money into some key races ahead of election day on 3 November.

The top individual donor is billionaire businessman Elon Musk, who has spent almost half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates, particularly in Texas where many of his companies are based.

BBC Verify has looked into the figures and where the money was spent.

There are rules on how much people, parties and political action committees (Pacs) can give directly to candidates.

But Super Pacs can accept unlimited contributions from individuals, corporations, labour unions, and other political committees. They can't give that money directly to candidates but they can spend it supporting them indirectly.

According to the latest Federal Election Commission , external (FEC) filings which run to mid-October, more than $9.5bn had been spent in this midterms cycle.

Pacs and Super Pacs make up more than half of that - at about $5.5bn - with their spending in the last couple of months almost doubling.

Candidates, parties and outside groups have to report their spending to the FEC, but the full totals won't be available until after the midterm elections.

However, Open Secrets has projected the total will be $11.9bn based on trends in past cycles.

This would be about 30% more than what was spent during the last midterm elections in 2022.

The top 40 donors gave $2.4bn up until 14 October, according to the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice , external , which is a record high for that point in a midterms cycle.

"Spending in the 2026 midterms is shattering records, with more of the money coming from the wealthiest donors and groups this election," says Michael Beckel, a US campaign finance expert.

As well as individuals, organisations can also give to Pacs. For example, Geosor Corp and Fund for Policy Reform, both founded by the billionaire financier George Soros, have given a combined $102m to liberal groups.

Aside from Soros, former New York City mayor and businessman Michael Bloomberg has been the biggest Democratic donor, giving more than $60m.

Several billionaires including Jeff Yass, who runs one of the world's largest trading firms, and Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, the owners of a US business supply company, have given over $100m this campaign to Republican causes, according to FEC filings.

But Musk has given by far the most of any individual, donating almost half a billion dollars as of October.

Musk has given most of this to a Super Pac he set up in 2024 called America PAC, as well as to the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund.

Most of his money has been spent on the Texas Senate race, supporting Republican candidate Ken Paxton, who is running against Democratic candidate James Talarico.

America PAC's investments in the Texas race total more than $45m. It has also invested around $10m into both of the Senate races in Michigan and Ohio.

"Crypto companies have also been very active this cycle, with Ripple and Coinbase combining to give $63 million to fund Super Pacs promoting the crypto industry's interests," says Brendan J Glavin of Open Secrets.

Campaigns and political groups spend money trying to reach voters in a variety of ways - including hiring staff to do on-the-ground voter outreach and hosting campaign events like rallies. They also spend money to conduct internal polling.

However, the majority of funds are spent on advertising - especially on TV.

In this cycle, $11.15bn has been spent on advertising up until the end of October, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact , external .

"Traditional broadcast television remains the top beneficiary of advertising expenditures, though expenditures on digital ads continue to increase," says Beckel.

Similarly to Musk's spending, AdImpact tracked that most of the money has been spent on advertising in the Senate races in Michigan, Texas and Ohio, followed by Iowa and Maine.

items.title: Man guilty of stealing cash from farm owned by South African president
items.summary: The case, part of the "Farmgate" scandal, has left President Cyril Ramaphosa mired in an impeachment saga.
items.content:
A court in South Africa has found a man guilty of stealing more than $580,000 (£432,000) in cash from a farm owned by South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, in a case that mired the head of state in an impeachment saga.

Imanuwela David was found guilty of theft on Monday, as well as conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal at Phala Phala farm in the Limpopo province in 2020.

Froliana Joseph, a cleaner at the property, was also found guilty of conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal.

Her brother, Ndilinasho Joseph, was acquitted on all charges.

David was accused of breaking into the cattle farm in February 2020 and taking the cash from a sofa on the property. David then went on a spending spree, buying a range of cars including three Mercedes - among them one for his girlfriend - a Porsche, two Volkswagens as well as diamond-encrusted Rolex watches and a house.

David told the court he had made the money through businesses including diamonds and Bitcoin, claims the court rejected. The court also found that David was the only one of the two convicted who had any of the stolen cash in his bank account.

There have been many twists and turns in what is known as the Farmgate scandal.

The theft was largely unknown until 2022 when it was brought to light by Arthur Fraser, South Africa's former intelligence chief and an ally for the former president Jacob Zuma, when he claimed that Ramaphosa hid the theft from the police and tax authorities.

Ramaphosa admitted the theft took place but denied any wrongdoing.

An independent panel that same year found Ramaphosa could have questions to answer over the burglary. MPs voted against establishing an impeachment inquiry.

In May this year, the constitutional court ruled that parliament had acted unlawfully by shelving the panel's report, and in July Ramaphosa blocked the parliamentary inquiry through a provincial court.

The cash-in-the-sofa saga that just won't go away for South Africa's president

items.title: FI apre a mini-ritocchi sulle pensioni. Ma è rebus coperture
items.summary: Al via l'iter della manovra, pure scuola e sanità nel mirino. Tagli anche sulle calamità
items.content:
Si lamentano, per ora sottovoce, le Regioni, comprese quelle a guida centrodestra. Si lamentano gli editori e librerie, per la novità sui testi scolastici da stampare direttamente dalla versione online. Si lamentano gli infermieri, e financo la sanità privata, i Vigili del Fuoco, i militari, per le disparità con le forze di polizia. E' in agitazione il comparto della scuola, pronto allo sciopero, e sono in grande allarme i sindacati per i tagli alle rivalutazioni degli assegni. E se sulle pensioni qualche spiraglio lo apre Forza Italia, resta la consapevolezza, come ammette lo stesso Antonio Tajani, che "tutto non si può fare", che la situazione internazionale resta più complessa che mai e i margini, negoziati con l'Europa, già tirati al massimo.

Mentre si è aperta formalmente, alla Camera, la sessione di Bilancio, già piovono critiche da tutte le parti alla quinta manovra firmata da Giorgia Meloni e Giancarlo Giorgetti. Ora sarà la volta degli stralci delle materie considerate estranee al disegno di legge di Bilancio, che la commissione guidata da Giuseppe Mangialavori (FI) dovrebbe affrontare già mercoledì, quando sarà deciso il ciclo di audizioni completo e la scadenza per gli emendamenti - che potrebbe essere attorno al 17-18 novembre.

Sarà poi la conferenza dei capigruppo a fine mese a stabilire la deadline per l'approdo in Aula, ma già tra i deputati si scommette su un ok a ridosso di Natale (tra il 21 e il 23 dicembre). Con buona pace dei senatori che, con ogni probabilità, dovranno rientrare dalla pausa natalizia per l'ok definitivo - e senza margini per ulteriori interventi - prima di Capodanno. Un film già visto, oramai un classico di fine anno. Ciononostante, in assenza di incontri con le parti sociali prima del varo, i partiti scaldano i motori per provare a incidere nel passaggio parlamentare. Forza Italia inizia dalla segretaria generale della Cisl, Daniela Fumarola, che Tajani incontra al partito con i due capigruppo, Stefania Craxi e Enrico Costa.

"Non possiamo stravolgere la manovra", è la premessa del vicepremier e leader azzurro, che promette poi ai suoi interlocutori che FI - che ribadisce la priorità di introdurre la previdenza dedicata per le forze armate - "studierà tutte le possibilità" sia con propri emendamenti sia "attraverso una valutazione che verrà fatta anche all'interno della maggioranza", convinto che "sulle pensioni qualche risultato si possa ottenere". Difficile, comunque, senza trovare coperture alternative alla nuova stretta sulle rivalutazioni degli assegni che scatta per le pensioni oltre 4 volte il minimo.

Una manovra "da rapina sociale", la bolla il leader di Avs Angelo Bonelli, mentre i colleghi del Pd, che puntano il dito contro la riduzione progressiva dei fondi per la sanità rispetto al Pil, hanno già iniziato a loro volta a incontrare le parti sociali. I primi incontri sono stati, spiegano fonti dem, con Legacoop e Ance, ma altri ce ne saranno di qui a quando i lavori sulla manovra entreranno nel vivo. Nuove coperture, in ogni caso, non saranno facili da trovare. La coperta dei fondi per le modifiche parlamentari è cortissima, 120 milioni nel 2027 e altrettanti nel 2028. E già si è raschiato tutto il raschiabile, tra razionalizzazioni, tagli e rinvii, come quelli sugli interventi di pubblica calamità del soccorso civile: 1,2 miliardi di riduzione delle dotazioni nel triennio, che saranno sì ripristinate, ma dal 2030.

La maggioranza, per ora, difende l'impianto della legge di Bilancio, anche dalle proteste della scuola: è "l'ennesima menzogna della sinistra", dice il meloniano Raffaele Speranzon, perché "a causa della denatalità la popolazione scolastica subisce un calo dell'1,5% l'anno" mentre la manovra copre "il 99,5% del turnover dei docenti". Quindi ci sarà addirittura "un aumento di cattedre per studente rispetto al passato". Ma intanto i sindacati chiedono di cancellare i tagli. O sarà sciopero.

items.title: Ci sono malfunzionamenti anche in supermercati italiani, probabilmente dovuti ad attacchi informatici
items.content:
Lunedì ci sono stati malfunzionamenti ai frigoriferi di alcuni supermercati in Sicilia, Emilia-Romagna e Toscana. Decine di episodi analoghi erano stati segnalati a partire dalla mattina in altri sette paesi europei. Giuseppe Spadaro, direttore generale di un gruppo che gestisce supermercati a marchio Coop in diverse città della Sicilia, ha detto all’ Ansa che «si sono verificati attacchi hacker» ai sistemi di refrigerazione dei banchi alimentari di almeno quattro negozi, tre a Catania e uno a Palermo.

L’Agenzia per la cybersicurezza nazionale (ACN) ha ricevuto una notifica di un attacco simile da parte un’azienda toscana del settore della ristorazione, e ha rilevato un attacco informatico anche in un’impresa emiliana della produzione di surgelati. L’ACN ha raccomandato alle aziende di verificare urgentemente che i sistemi utilizzati per controllare e gestire i frigoriferi a distanza non siano accessibili dall’esterno tramite internet.

Fin dalla mattina erano stati segnalati malfunzionamenti anche in diversi supermercati di Svezia, Irlanda, Belgio, Lussemburgo, Paesi Bassi, Estonia e Finlandia. Varie aziende hanno parlato esplicitamente di attacchi informatici contro gli impianti di refrigerazione, in cui in alcuni casi le temperature sono state impostate su 50 gradi centigradi, facendo andare a male il cibo. La situazione ricorda gli episodi avvenuti in Francia tre settimane fa, quando i congelatori e i frigoriferi di centinaia di supermercati erano stati messi fuori uso .

items.title: Il telescopio spaziale Swift della Nasa in caduta libera, il rientro tra il 3 e 4 novembre
items.summary: Brucerà nell'atmosfera, ma detriti potrebbero cadere lungo la fascia equatoriale
items.content:
Atteso fra il 3 e il 4 novembre il rientro incontrollato nell’atmosfera del telescopio spaziale Swift della Nasa, pesante 1,5 tonnellate: gran parte del telescopio brucerà nell’atmosfera ma non si può escludere che qualche frammento possa arrivare al suolo. Non ci sono pericoli per l’Ital ia, i frammenti potranno cadere solo in una fascia attorno all’equatore , e quasi certamente in mare o zone disabitate.

Dopo oltre 20 anni di attività nell’osservare uno dei più enigmatici fenomeni del cosmo, i cosiddetti lampi di raggi gamma, e un ultimo disperato tentativo di salvataggio fallito – con il mancato funzionamento del 'carro attrezzi spaziale' Link – l’osservatorio Swift si prepara a distruggersi nell’atmosfera. Secondo gli ultimi dati il telescopio è sceso ben oltre i 275 chilometri di altezza già da vari giorni e l’atmosfera, che scendendo diventa via via più densa, lo sta rapidamente rallentando e facendo scendere di quota. Una volta che arriverà intorno ai 120 chilometri di altezza l’intera struttura dovrebbe iniziare rapidamente a scaldarsi e scendere sempre più velocemente : i primi elementi a bruciare e staccarsi saranno le antenne e i pannelli solari mentre il resto del corpo principale dovrebbe frammentarsi e vaporizzarsi, a causa del calore, intorno ai 78 chilometri.

Una scia di fuoco che potrebbe essere visibile anche in pieno giorno, con una magnitudine compresa tra -8 e -10 sottolinea il sito specializzato Spaceweather.com, mentre alcuni frammenti più compatti, come i volani rotanti usati per indirizzare il satellite, potrebbero raggiungere il suolo, ma quasi certamente in mare o zone disabitate. L’area di caduta è una fascia compresa tra + e - 21 gradi rispetto all’equatore, molto lontana dall’Italia, e secondo la Nasa la caduta è stimata alle 17:18 ora italiana del 3 novembre con un margine di incertezza di 12 ore, prima o dopo.

items.title: Maltempo al Centro Sud, nevicate, allagamenti e scuole chiuse
items.summary: Cede un tetto a Crotone. Trani al buio per un fulmine. Stop alle lezioni a Chieti e Pescara
items.content:
Era ampiamente previsto e annunciato, ma ha ugualmente prodotto effetti imprevisti il maltempo che per l'intera giornata ha interessato il Centro-Sud Italia, in particolare sul versante adriatico e ionico. Sospese le attività didattiche in molte località a seguito di temporali che hanno provocato allagamenti e trasformato le strade in fiumi di fango . Unico dato suggestivo le cime imbiancate sull'Appennino, in particolare in alcune località sciistiche in Abruzzo, regione dove peraltro la neve aveva fatto la sua comparsa un paio di settimane fa sulla Maiella.

In Calabria, per puro miracolo non ci sono stati feriti a Crotone dove a mezzogiorno il tetto di un condominio, divelto da forti raffiche di vento, è caduto sulla centralissima via Mario Nicoletta, vicino al palazzo della Provincia . La copertura, composta da lamiere pesanti e taglienti, ha urtato la facciata di un edificio di fronte prima di finire su alcune auto in sosta e sulla carreggiata. Danni anche all'illuminazione pubblica. Vigili del fuoco, Protezione civile regionale e Polizia locale hanno delimitato l'area per poter rimuovere i detriti. In Puglia , Trani è rimasta per circa un'ora senza corrente elettrica per un guasto a una cabina primaria di alimentazione alla periferia della città, probabilmente a causa di un fulmine.

In vista dell'allerta meteo arancione diversi Comuni, dal Foggiano al Salento, avevano disposto la chiusura di scuole, cimiteri e parchi. Annullate molte cerimonie previste per la ricorrenza del 2 novembre. In Abruzzo, temporali e piogge insistenti hanno determinato la sospensione delle attività didattiche in presenza all'Università d'Annunzio di Chieti e Pescara: martedì si farà ricorso alla Dad. E a Chieti le scuole di ogni ordine e grado domani saranno chiuse: il sindaco ha emesso apposita ordinanza, edifici aperti solo per le attività amministrative.

Sempre a Chieti infiltrazioni di acqua hanno interessato l'ospedale, in particolare la Medicina nucleare e la Radioterapia: qui sono stati effettuati tutti i trattamenti programmati nella mattinata, ma sono state rinviate le sedute del pomeriggio. Disagi e allagamenti per l'intera giornata a Pescara e nell'area metropolitana dove la pioggia è caduta quasi ininterottamente per dodici ore. Molte le strade chiuse per l'intera mattinata nel capoluogo adriatico dove nel pomeriggio una grossa quercia è crollata in strada in via Passo della Portella , senza fortunatamente coinvolgere pedoni o automobilisti.

E dal pomeriggio in Abruzzo due fiumi fanno registrare "il superamento della soglia di pre-allarme e un graduale aumento verso la soglia di allarme", il Pescara e l'Aterno-Sagittario. Per questo il Centro funzionale della Protezione civile raccomanda ai Comuni di "mettere in atto le azioni previste nel Piano Comunale di Emergenza".

items.title: Egoless Mathematics in the AI Era
items.summary: Article URL: https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/11/02/egoless-mathematics-in-the-ai-era/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50341736 Points: 159 # Comments: 118
items.content:
[This is a guest post by Karthik C. S. , Amit Sahai , and Jie Xue . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

This is a good time for mathematicians to think carefully about the purpose of their work. The development of artificial intelligence brings that question before us with unusual force. Much of the discussion concerns which tasks machines will perform and which abilities will remain distinctively human. But our response also depends on a prior question: what do we understand mathematical work to be, and what gives it its worth? If our answer has become inseparable from the production of results and the demonstration of individual ability, the present uncertainty may reveal a difficulty in our conception of the work itself.

There are broadly two perspectives on mathematics. According to one, we invent it as we construct it: we introduce concepts, choose axioms, and develop theories. According to the other, mathematics exists independently of these activities, and our task is to discover it. These perspectives need not disagree about every aspect of mathematical practice. We plainly develop formalism and arguments. The deeper question is whether the truths we come to understand owe their existence to these acts, or whether our constructions enable us to recognize something that does not depend on us.

While discovery of mathematical truth can sound passive, a paleontologist searching for fossils must decide where to excavate, develop techniques, and recognize the significance of incomplete remains. The fossils existed long before the investigation, but finding them may require extraordinary imagination. Their prior existence gives direction to the investigator’s activity. Similarly, a mathematical discovery may require the invention of an entire language and framework through which a previously unnoticed relationship becomes intelligible. The discovery may require great creativity, but that does not make the truth discovered a creation of the individual. We encounter this distinction whenever our constructions surprise us. A definition introduced for one purpose reveals an unexpected connection elsewhere. A conjecture that seemed to organize our examples admits a counterexample. Two theories developed through different questions turn out to express a common structure. In each case, our thought encounters something it did not freely determine. We can revise our definitions or abandon our conjecture, but we cannot make the original argument valid merely by wishing it so.

The Platonic perspective gives a natural account of this independence. On this view, there were infinitely many primes before anyone proved that fact. Mathematical truth neither waits for our recognition nor receives its authority from it. We may choose how to describe a structure, but we do not choose its properties in the same way. This perspective also changes the place of the mathematician. Our intelligence becomes a means through which an order independent of us can be understood. The significance of the work lies in its relation to that order.

The distinction between a correct derivation and an understanding of its significance is equally important. An axiomatic system permits indefinitely many deductions, but the ability to produce them does not by itself supply a worthy direction of inquiry. Mathematical statements may be formally correct without being enlightening. We can introduce countless definitions and prove countless statements about them. What makes one definition illuminating? Why does one theorem disclose something fundamental while another merely adds to the available material? These questions concern the relation of a particular investigation to the principles it brings into view. Mathematical taste has a place here, provided we understand it as more than individual preference. We value a theory when it reveals a unity among things previously understood separately, or enables us to recognize why a phenomenon occurs. Although mathematical truths may exist independently of us, their discovery can transform our understanding and enrich our experience of the world. The ability to carry out longer chains of reasoning does not by itself explain such understanding. Reasoning serves understanding by articulating relationships and making their justification explicit. However, the success of reasoning does not mean that all knowledge can be reduced to it. Nor does our ability to reason more extensively determine what is worth knowing or why we seek knowledge.

Mathematics is only one field of knowledge. Not everything can be understood mathematically, nor is mathematical achievement the ultimate purpose of intellectual life. Yet we increasingly measure intellectual life through publications, citations, awards, and other indicators of performance. While useful, these measures become problematic when they define the worth of the work itself. We begin to see mathematicians as collections of productive abilities, and mathematics as merely their output. From this perspective, anxiety about being replaced by AI is natural: a machine that performs these tasks better appears to threaten our worth. But the problem began before AI arrived. We had already come to understand ourselves in terms suited to machines. AI merely exposes the consequences of this view.

The response cannot simply be to seek refuge in distinctively human abilities such as creativity, intuition, or taste. If we value these abilities primarily because they give us an advantage over machines, we remain trapped in the same conception of intellectual worth. Why should the value of our pursuit depend on being better at it than someone or something else?

Mathematics offers an opportunity to reconsider this whole orientation. Its truths do not become more true through the distinction of the person who expresses them. In understanding a proof, we bring our thought into conformity with a relationship whose validity does not belong to us. The particular path by which we arrive may bear the marks of our individuality. What is understood is available beyond that individuality. We can allow this experience to loosen the belief that knowledge has its highest value as an achievement attributable to ourselves.

Egoless mathematics begins with taking that possibility seriously. Humility then reaches beyond modesty about our accomplishments or generosity in sharing credit. It concerns the place from which we pursue knowledge. We may seek truth to serve our existing purposes, or allow what we discover to change those purposes themselves. If we approach truth on the condition that its discovery must preserve our importance, we have already made it subordinate to ourselves. Accomplishing this reordering can be demanding, as intellectual sophistication can furnish elaborate defenses of the very attachments that prevent us from understanding. What matters is whether our abilities remain answerable to truth, including when it requires us to reconsider what we have been using those abilities for.

From this perspective, the possibility of mathematical discoveries through AI need not be a source of sadness about our purpose. A truth has become accessible; its worth is not diminished by the absence of our authorship. We need not immediately turn the event into a judgment about our relative importance. The search can continue without requiring every advance to vindicate the seeker. Indeed, the demand for such vindication has always burdened the pursuit, whether the competing claim came from another mathematician or from a machine.

The opportunity before us is therefore more substantial than a rearrangement of mathematical labor. It invites us to reconsider what gives an intellectual life its worth, and to let the pursuit of truth shape not only our work but also how we approach life.

This may sound like asking us all to become saints. Insofar as it asks us to grow in virtue and relinquish our attachment to our own importance, that impression is not far from the truth. But virtue is not something to cultivate for the admiration of others. It is necessary for genuine joy, even in our work. The satisfaction of solving a difficult problem or winning a prize can be fleeting when it rests on our standing relative to others. The joy of understanding is different. Something previously obscure becomes clear, and we recognize a beauty that does not diminish when someone else discovers it first. We can share this joy without depriving anyone of it. Growing in virtue allows us to experience it more fully, free from the need to establish our own importance.

This perspective may also help reconcile two positions within the mathematical community regarding AI. Some are comfortable with or even enthusiastic about using AI , but wish to develop appropriate processes and principles for its use. Others prefer not to use AI at all . Both positions have their merits. Egoless mathematics offers a way of reconciling them by introducing a higher consideration: both approaches can reflect the same underlying commitment to mathematical truth, regardless of how we choose to pursue it. Our aim here is not to settle particular questions of policy, but to develop a higher-level perspective that can guide our deliberations and ultimately our actions.

items.title: I Laburisti britannici hanno rivisto i criteri per la richiesta del permesso di soggiorno permanente, ma non per tutti
items.content:
La ministra dell’Interno britannica Shabana Mahmood ha annunciato l’ammorbidimento di alcune misure sull’immigrazione che erano state presentate alla fine del 2025 dal governo Laburista del Regno Unito, molto restrittive anche per gli standard della politica britannica.

Le misure riguardano centinaia di migliaia di persone che nel tempo sono arrivate legalmente nel Regno Unito e che vogliono chiedere il permesso di soggiorno permanente. Attualmente bisogna attendere cinque anni per farne richiesta: con le nuove regole bisognerà di norma invece attenderne dieci. Dopo uno scontro interno al partito e tra le pressioni dei sindacati, tuttavia, per certe categorie di lavoratori stranieri il limite è stato abbassato.

Quelli che guadagnano più di 125mila sterline l’anno o con certi tipi di visto potranno fare richiesta dopo tre anni. Altri a reddito più basso o certi dipendenti pubblici, come medici, insegnanti, infermieri o personale sanitario con mansioni di cura potranno invece farlo dopo cinque: dovranno però avere un ottimo livello di inglese, nessun precedente penale, nessun debito con l’erario, e aver dimostrato di pagare un’assicurazione nel Regno Unito.

Secondo le stime dei media britannici, la misura riguarderebbe quasi 300mila persone. La maggior parte delle norme proposte nel 2025 comunque è stata confermata, compresa quella che impone a chi arriva nel Regno Unito in maniera illegale di aspettare fino a 30 anni per poter chiedere il permesso di soggiorno permanente.

items.title: Ubuntu still has not released patch for Linux 0day RCE in almost 3 weeks
items.summary: Article URL: https://freenode.net/article/ubuntu-lts-kernels-still-unfixed-for-critical-cve-2026-98432 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50341462 Points: 505 # Comments: 142
items.content:
No patched kernels are available yet for 22.04, 24.04, or 26.04 despite a CVSS 9.8 rating.

Ubuntu has not shipped fixed kernels for CVE-2026-98432 , a critical vulnerability scored CVSS 9.8, leaving the 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 LTS releases without a vendor update.

Operators running those releases therefore have no official kernel package that closes the hole. The gap matters most for internet-facing and multi-tenant self-hosted systems that rely on Ubuntu’s LTS kernels for isolation and privilege boundaries; until packages appear, those hosts remain exposed to whatever remote or local attack the CVE enables.

Ubuntu has not announced an ETA for the fixes. In the interim, affected administrators are left to decide whether to stay on the stock kernel, apply out-of-tree mitigations if any exist, or move workloads onto releases or kernels that already carry the patch.

items.title: Daniel come Tom Hanks in The Terminal, da settimane vive a Capodichino
items.summary: Dice di avere 25 anni, è senza documenti e appare disorientato. Ambasciata al lavoro
items.content:
Per settimane è passato quasi inosservato. Poi è diventato una presenza silenziosa ma costante nello scalo aeroportuale partenopeo. Un giovane alto, biondo, con gli occhi azzurri, che dice di chiamarsi Daniel, di avere 25 anni e di essere svedese. "Si confondeva tranquillamente tra i passeggeri", raccontano alcuni addetti alle pulizie. Poi, sono arrivate le domande: "Perché dorme sempre qui? C'è qualcuno che lo sta cercando? Ha bisogno di qualcosa?".

Raccontano alcuni lavoratori: "Volevamo fare una colletta per aiutarlo a tornare a casa, ma il problema è che non riuscivamo neanche a capire dove volesse tornare. Ci chiediamo spesso se ci sia una famiglia che lo sta cercando disperatamente". Da lui, però, sono sempre arrivate poche parole e quasi nessuna richiesta. Una riservatezza che ha reso difficile ricostruirne la storia. Ad alcuni avrebbe anche raccontato di essere stato picchiato e derubato prima di arrivare a Napoli, lamentando dolori alle mani e alla testa. Circostanze che, al momento, non trovano riscontri indipendenti. Il 15 ottobre il caso era stato segnalato al console onorario di Svezia, Pierluigi Petrone, che ha incontrato il ragazzo. "L'ambasciata sta lavorando per arrivare a una soluzione", ha spiegato, sottolineando le difficoltà nell'accertarne l'identità.

items.title: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
items.summary: Dozens of shops across European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their fridges.
items.content:
Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.

Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.

And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.

However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.

Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.

But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.

Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.

"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.

He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible.

"I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.

Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.

The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.

However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.

That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.

The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.

Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.

It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.

When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.

Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.

Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility.

"The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.

He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace.

"Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said.

"Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."

Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.

Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security.

"Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.

Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.

Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.

His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.

Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.
